week_headline: Sedentary lifestyles and women's nutrition take centre stage as new research links prolonged sitting to cancer mortality and doctors push omega-3 rich diets

top10.claim: Prolonged Sitting Linked to Higher Cancer Death Risk , Study Finds – NaturalNews . com
top10.verdict: There is genuine, peer-reviewed evidence linking prolonged sedentary behaviour to increased cancer mortality risk — studies published in JAMA Oncology and JNCI do support this association. However, NaturalNews.com is a notoriously unreliable outlet known for sensationalising research, so the framing likely overstates the strength or novelty of the finding. The core science is real, but the source deserves healthy scepticism — seek the original study rather than the news wrap.
top10.verdict_highlight: Real science, but check the original study
sources: JAMA Oncology – Sedentary Behaviour and Cancer Mortality (2020)
Journal of the National Cancer Institute – Physical Inactivity and Cancer Risk
WHO Global Guidelines on Physical Activity and Sedentary Behaviour (2020)
American Cancer Society – Physical Activity and Cancer
top10.global_opinion: In the US, public health bodies like the CDC have increasingly incorporated sedentary behaviour warnings into cancer prevention guidelines, reflecting growing research consensus. In the UK, the NHS and Public Health England acknowledge sitting time as a risk factor but tend to frame it within broader physical inactivity guidance rather than isolating cancer risk specifically. In Australia, the national physical activity guidelines explicitly call out prolonged sitting as an independent health risk, making them among the more direct globally.
top10.brit_take: Turns out all those years of being told to get off the sofa were medically justified — though your mum probably didn't need a study to know that.

top10.claim: Fatty fish should be a part of your regular diet : Physician Dr Kunal Sood lists 5 healthy habits women should know about
top10.verdict: Fatty fish like salmon, mackerel, and sardines are genuinely well-supported by research — they're rich in omega-3 fatty acids, vitamin D, and high-quality protein, all of which benefit cardiovascular health, brain function, and inflammation reduction, with particular relevance to women's hormonal and bone health. The claim is solidly grounded in nutrition science, though framing it as advice specifically for women adds a layer of context that isn't always strongly differentiated from general population advice. It's good, practical guidance — just not uniquely revolutionary for women.
top10.verdict_highlight: Fatty fish benefits are well-evidenced for most people
sources: Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health – The Nutrition Source: Omega-3 Fatty Acids
Journal of Nutrition – Omega-3s and Cardiovascular Health
NIH Office of Dietary Supplements – Omega-3 Fatty Acids Fact Sheet
BMJ – Fish Consumption and Cardiovascular Disease Meta-analysis
EFSA – Scientific Opinion on Dietary Reference Values for Fats
top10.global_opinion: In Japan, fatty fish consumption is deeply embedded in the diet and widely credited by researchers as a contributor to the country's low cardiovascular disease rates and longevity — the science and culture align here unusually well. In Nordic countries like Norway and Sweden, government dietary guidelines actively recommend oily fish multiple times per week, backed by strong national research programmes. In parts of South Asia and Sub-Africa where fatty fish is less accessible or culturally common, public health messaging tends to focus on alternative omega-3 sources like flaxseed and walnuts.
top10.brit_take: The British have been eating fish on Fridays for centuries without needing a physician's five-point plan — though swapping battered cod for mackerel might be worth considering.
